clades.name: Amniota
clades.sum: Tetrapods whose embryos develop inside protective membranes: reptiles (including birds) and mammals with their extinct relatives.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Amniota, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Embryo enclosed by three extra-embryonic membranes: amnion, chorion and allantois
No aquatic larval stage; development is direct
Thick, keratinized skin
Breathing by movements of the rib cage (costal ventilation)
clades.notes: Defined as the smallest crown clade containing humans, the Greek tortoise and the Nile crocodile. Amniotes arose from reptiliomorph tetrapods in the Carboniferous and split almost at once into Synapsida and Sauropsida; molecular dates for the split cluster around 310–340 million years ago. Older clawed footprints from Australia have been proposed as amniote tracks, but the claim is disputed.

clades.name: Amorphea
clades.sum: Eukaryote supergroup made of the Amoebozoa and the Obazoa — the latter including opisthokonts (animals and fungi) and their protist relatives.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “Amorphea”, revision 1382799800 (supergroup; name recommended in 2012 by the International Society of Protistologists)
diag: A fusion of three genes for pyrimidine synthesis (carbamoyl phosphate synthase, dihydroorotase, aspartate carbamoyltransferase) absent in other eukaryotes
Cells typically with two basal bodies, of which only one usually bears a flagellum
clades.notes: Proposed by Cavalier-Smith (2002) as the "unikonts"; renamed Amorphea in 2012 because the supposed single flagellum was found not to be a true shared feature. Its sister group in most analyses is Diphoda (plants, algae and many protists). The internal classification of its smaller lineages (apusomonads, breviates, "Sulcozoa") is still being revised.

clades.name: Archaea
clades.sum: Single-celled prokaryotes forming one of the two primary branches of cellular life; eukaryotes arose from within them.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “Archaea”, revision 1385819730 (treated as a domain; the PBDB record named Archaea is an unrelated spider genus)
diag: Cell membranes built from ether-linked lipids, unlike the ester-linked lipids of bacteria and eukaryotes
A distinctive rotary swimming organ, the archaellum
Genes and pathways for DNA transcription and translation closer to those of eukaryotes than of bacteria
Metabolisms unknown in other life, such as methanogenesis
clades.notes: First separated from bacteria as "archaebacteria" on the basis of ribosomal RNA (Woese and colleagues). Classification is unstable because most lineages are known only from environmental gene sequences. In the strict cladistic sense Archaea includes the eukaryotes, which branch from within the Asgard archaea; in everyday use the name still means the prokaryotic members only. No archaeal cell fossils can be identified with confidence; the deep record relies on chemical fossils (lipids).

clades.name: Archelosauria
clades.sum: Turtles and archosaurs (crocodilians and birds) with their extinct relatives, to the exclusion of lepidosaurs.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Archelosauria, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Supported mainly by molecular data: about 1,000 ultraconserved genome elements shared by turtles and archosaurs but not lepidosaurs
Recent morphological analyses also place turtles (Pantestudines) inside Archosauromorpha
clades.notes: Named by Crawford et al. (2015). Morphology long placed turtles elsewhere — with parareptiles, outside Sauria, or with lepidosaurs — so turtle origins remain one of the main questions about the group.

clades.name: Archosauria
clades.sum: The crown group of birds and crocodilians: everything descended from their last common ancestor, including dinosaurs and pterosaurs.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Archosauria, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Teeth set in deep sockets
Antorbital and mandibular fenestrae
A pronounced fourth trochanter on the femur
clades.notes: Defined as a crown group, it splits at its base into Pseudosuchia (the crocodile line) and Avemetatarsalia (the bird line). Many classic features are also found in close relatives outside the crown, such as proterosuchids and euparkeriids, which were formerly called archosaurs.

clades.name: Archosauriformes
clades.sum: Archosaurs and their nearest relatives, such as proterosuchids, erythrosuchids and euparkeriids.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Archosauriformes, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: An antorbital fenestra (opening in front of the eye)
Serrated teeth set in deep sockets
clades.notes: Defined by Gauthier as the clade from the last common ancestor of Proterosuchidae and Archosauria; later definitions use Proterosuchus with archosaurs or with Gallus and Alligator. The group originated in the Late Permian and survived the end-Permian extinction. Many of its members were formerly lumped as "thecodonts", a paraphyletic group no longer used.

clades.name: Archosauromorpha
clades.sum: Diapsid reptiles closer to archosaurs than to lepidosaurs, from Permian long-necked forms to crocodilians, dinosaurs and birds.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Archosauromorpha, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Laminae (thin bony sheets) on the vertebrae
A posterodorsal process on the premaxilla
clades.notes: Named by von Huene in 1946 but little used until cladistic studies of the 1980s. Main groups: allokotosaurs, rhynchosaurs, Archosauriformes and a polyphyletic set of long-necked forms (Protorosaurus, tanystropheids, Prolacerta); turtles and choristoderes are placed here by some authors. First records are Middle–Late Permian.

clades.name: Asgardarchaeota
clades.sum: Archaea whose genomes carry many "eukaryotic signature proteins"; the eukaryotes evolved from within this group.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “Asgard archaea”, revision 1385819849 (kingdom Promethearchaeati, formerly the superphylum or phylum "Asgardarchaeota")
diag: Genes for proteins previously thought to be exclusive to eukaryotes (eukaryotic signature proteins)
Histone proteins with N-terminal tails, as in eukaryotes, in some members (Heimdallarchaeia)
Mostly known from environmental genomes; the few cultured members live in close metabolic partnership with bacteria
clades.notes: Its formal name under the prokaryote code is now kingdom Promethearchaeati, with the former "phyla" demoted to classes. Analyses differ on exactly where eukaryotes branch: some place them inside Heimdallarchaeia, a 2025 study places them outside it. The group supports a two-domain tree of life (Bacteria and Archaea, with eukaryotes nested in the latter). The cultured species Promethearchaeum syntrophicum was isolated in 2020.

clades.name: Avemetatarsalia
clades.sum: The bird line of archosaurs: everything closer to birds than to crocodilians, including dinosaurs and pterosaurs.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Avemetatarsalia, informal), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: "Advanced mesotarsal" ankle with a large astragalus and a small calcaneum working as a single hinge
Upright limbs held under the body
Filamentous body coverings in many members, from pterosaur pycnofibres to dinosaur feathers
clades.notes: Named by Benton (1999); also called Pan-Aves. Gauthier's earlier names Ornithosuchia and Ornithodira cover similar ground. Besides dinosaurs and pterosaurs, it includes Triassic lagerpetids, aphanosaurs and other early dinosauromorphs. Only dinosaurs and pterosaurs survived the end of the Triassic.

clades.name: Bilateria
clades.sum: Animals with a left–right symmetric body built around a head-to-tail axis: more than 98% of known animal species.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Bilateria, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Bilateral symmetry at least in the embryo (echinoderms become five-rayed as adults)
Three germ layers: endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm
Usually a through gut with separate mouth and anus
Cephalization: sense organs and nerve ganglia concentrated at the front end
clades.notes: Named by Hatschek in 1888. Traditionally divided into protostomes (now split into Ecdysozoa and Spiralia) and deuterostomes; whether Xenacoelomorpha belong at the base of the group, and whether deuterostomes are a natural group, are still argued. Bilaterians diversified rapidly in the late Ediacaran and Cambrian.

clades.name: Chordata
clades.sum: Animals with a notochord, a hollow dorsal nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, an endostyle and a post-anal tail at some stage of life: lancelets, tunicates and vertebrates.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Chordata, phylum), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Notochord: a stiff, elastic rod along the body axis
Hollow dorsal nerve cord (neural tube)
Pharyngeal slits
Endostyle, or the thyroid gland derived from it
Post-anal tail
clades.notes: Three subphyla: Cephalochordata (lancelets), Tunicata and Vertebrata; tunicates and vertebrates together form Olfactores. Two conserved protein insertions/deletions are shared by all chordates and no other animals. Tunicates keep the chordate features only as larvae. The phylum name is credited to Haeckel (1874).

clades.name: Deuterostomia
clades.sum: Bilaterians whose embryonic blastopore typically becomes the anus: chordates, echinoderms, hemichordates and extinct relatives.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Deuterostomia, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: The mouth forms at a second opening; the blastopore becomes the anus
Coelom formed by out-pocketing of the gut (enterocoely)
Radial, mostly indeterminate cleavage of the early embryo
More than 30 genes found in no other animal group
clades.notes: Named by Grobben (1908). Lophophorates and arrow worms, once included, were moved to the protostomes by molecular studies from 1995 on. Deuterostome-type development also occurs in some protostomes, so the group is now defined by molecular phylogeny rather than embryology alone.

clades.name: Diapsida
clades.sum: Reptiles that have, at least ancestrally, two openings on each side of the skull behind the eye: all living reptiles and birds and many extinct groups.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Diapsida, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Two temporal fenestrae (upper and lower) on each side of the skull, at least ancestrally
In neodiapsids, an upper temporal fenestra added to an already present lower one
clades.notes: Some members lost one or both openings (lizards, snakes, turtles) or reshaped the skull (birds) but remain diapsids by descent. The skull-opening classes of older classifications (Anapsida, Euryapsida) are no longer used as groups. Whether the early Araeoscelidia acquired their openings independently of Neodiapsida is under study.

clades.name: Eukaryota
clades.sum: Organisms whose cells have a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and a cytoskeleton: animals, plants, fungi and the many lineages of protists.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Eukaryota, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: DNA enclosed in a nucleus bounded by a double membrane
Membrane-bound organelles, including mitochondria derived from an engulfed alphaproteobacterium
An internal cytoskeleton of actin and microtubules
Mitosis and, in most lineages, meiosis and sexual reproduction
clades.notes: Thought to have originated in the Paleoproterozoic from a partnership between an Asgard archaeon (host) and an aerobic alphaproteobacterium that became the mitochondrion; plastids came later from cyanobacteria. The traditional four kingdoms (animals, plants, fungi, protists) are replaced in phylogenomic studies by supergroups such as Amorphea and Diphoda; protists are a paraphyletic grade. In a two-domain view the Eukaryota sit inside Archaea.

clades.name: ParaHoxozoa
clades.sum: Animals with Hox/ParaHox genes: bilaterians, cnidarians and placozoans, leaving out sponges and comb jellies.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “ParaHoxozoa”, revision 1377051484 (clade)
diag: Hox/ParaHox genes of the ANTP class, which give the group its name
Several further gene classes absent in sponges and comb jellies (among them HNF, CUT, PROS and ZF)
clades.notes: The tree node is labelled ParaHoxozoa (id kept as "eumetazoa"). If comb jellies are the first animal branch, the older name Eumetazoa is sometimes used for this same group. Whether sponges or comb jellies are the sister of all other animals is unresolved, so the base of the animal tree is shown as uncertain. A claim that sponges also have a ParaHox-like gene has been contested.

clades.name: Eureptilia
clades.sum: "True reptiles": diapsids, which include all living reptiles and birds, and several early Permo-Carboniferous forms such as captorhinids and Hylonomus.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Eureptilia, subclass), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Supraoccipital, tabular and supratemporal bones at the back of the skull greatly reduced
These reduced bones no longer in contact with the postorbital
clades.notes: One of the two traditional divisions of Sauropsida, with Parareptilia. Besides diapsids it held Permo-Carboniferous captorhinids and "protorothyrids" (Anthracodromeus is the oldest known climbing tetrapod); only diapsids outlived the Permian. Studies of the early 2020s found Parareptilia paraphyletic and recovered captorhinids and Protorothyris as stem amniotes rather than reptiles, so Eureptilia may not survive as a clade. Wikipedia has no separate article; the cited revision is the Sauropsida article.

clades.name: Gnathostomata
clades.sum: Jawed vertebrates — cartilaginous fishes, bony fishes and tetrapods, plus extinct placoderms and acanthodians — about 99% of living vertebrates.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Gnathostomata, superclass), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Jaws formed from the first pharyngeal arch
True teeth and paired pectoral and pelvic appendages
A horizontal semicircular canal in the inner ear
An adaptive immune system using V(D)J recombination, with thymus and spleen
clades.notes: The jawless osteostracans are generally taken as the closest relatives. Placoderms are now treated as a grade at the base of the group. The ancestor of jawed vertebrates went through two whole-genome duplications. Traditionally ranked as an infraphylum or superclass.

clades.name: Holozoa
clades.sum: Animals plus their closest single-celled relatives (choanoflagellates, filastereans, ichthyosporeans and others), to the exclusion of fungi.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Holozoa, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Animals and the unicellular choanoflagellates, filastereans, Pluriformea and Ichthyosporea share a common ancestor not shared with fungi (phylogenomic evidence)
Purely heterotrophic organisms
clades.notes: Holozoa replaces the older "Choanofila", which excluded animals and was therefore paraphyletic. The unicellular holozoans are studied to understand how multicellular animals arose. The order of the two earliest branches (Ichthyosporea and Pluriformea) is uncertain. Some Precambrian fossils once taken for animals may be holozoan protists.

clades.name: Metazoa
clades.sum: Animals: multicellular eukaryotes that feed on other organisms, develop through a blastula and, in most cases, can move.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Metazoa, subkingdom), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Cells embedded in an extracellular matrix of collagen and elastic glycoproteins
Embryos pass through a blastula, a hollow ball of cells
Muscle cells and, in nearly all groups, nerve cells
Heterotrophic: food is ingested and digested internally
clades.notes: Animals form a clade within Holozoa, closest to the choanoflagellates. The five main lineages are sponges, comb jellies, placozoans, cnidarians and bilaterians; which of sponges or comb jellies branched first is still debated. The first body fossils are Ediacaran; most living phyla appear during the Cambrian explosion about 539 million years ago.

clades.sum: Tunicates and vertebrates: all chordates except the lancelets.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Olfactores, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16

Neural-crest-like cells (rudimentary in tunicates, a true neural crest in vertebrates)
clades.notes: Since about 2006, molecular phylogenies have placed tunicates rather than lancelets as the closest relatives of vertebrates. Whether the common ancestor had a sedentary adult stage, as in many tunicates, is debated.

clades.name: Opisthokonta
clades.sum: The group uniting animals, fungi and their single-celled relatives, named for the single posterior flagellum that pushes their swimming cells.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Opisthokonta, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Flagellate cells (sperm, zoospores) driven by one posterior flagellum
Chitin produced outside the cell in walls, cysts or exoskeletons
Shared cellular and metabolic pathways supporting the animal–fungus split as its basal division

Its relationships were largely resolved by phylogenomics (Torruella et al. 2015). Together with apusomonads and breviates it forms Obazoa.

clades.name: Osteichthyes
clades.sum: Bony fishes in the cladistic sense: ray-finned and lobe-finned fishes and their descendants, the tetrapods.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Osteichthyes, class), downloaded 2026-11-16

Large dermal bones covering the head and shoulder girdle, with a stable pattern of skull bones
Lungs or a swim bladder derived from an outgrowth of the gut
Bony operculum covering the gills

home.title: Life on Earth
home.lead: Every organism in this atlas — from bacteria to pterosaurs — belongs to one family tree that goes back more than three and a half billion years.
intro: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, and life appeared early in its history: the oldest fossils that clearly record living things are stromatolites about 3.48 billion years old from the Dresser Formation of Western Australia. Older traces, chemical signals in rocks and crystals, may push the start back to 3.7 or even 4.1 billion years.

All living things share the same genetic code and the same molecular machinery for building proteins, which is why biologists accept that they descend from a single last universal common ancestor (LUCA). From it come three great lineages of cells: Bacteria, Archaea and eukaryotes — the organisms whose cells have a nucleus. Current evidence places the origin of eukaryotes inside the archaea, from a host related to today's Asgard archaea that took in a bacterium; the tree of this atlas follows that view.

For most of this history life was microscopic. Animals with complex bodies diversified rapidly from about 539 million years ago, in the Cambrian explosion, and the living world has since been reshaped by five major mass extinctions. The groups below give a glimpse of that diversity; each picture opens its place in the tree.
